To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the majority of cancer patients use some form of alternative medicine, and that most of them do not disclose this to their physicians.

(1) the majority of cancer patients do not disclose to their physicians the complementary/alternative products they are using; (2) the most common reasons for non-disclosure are fear of negative reaction from the physician and lack of knowledge about how to disclose; (3) the majority of patients are using complementary/alternative products to improve their health and well-being; (4) patients who use complementary/alternative products have a more positive attitude toward their cancer and its treatment and have a better quality of

the eight herbal products commonly used by cancer patient are not recommended by the National Cancer Institute and the American Cancer Society because of lack of evidence of efficacy, lack of evidence of safety, or both, and because of the possibility of harm to the patient.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the role of complementary/alternative therapies in the lives of patients with cancer, and with the development of effective strategies to help patients make informed decisions about the use of these therapies.
the development and implementation of an evidence-based model of care for cancer patients who are using herbal products and other complementary/alternative therapies.
the use of herbal medicines in cancer patients and their physicians.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is insufficient evidence to either support or refute the use of these eight herbal products for cancer.
the evidence for efficacy of these herbal preparations in the treatment of cancer is lacking.
the evidence for the effectiveness of these herbal products is insufficient to support their use in cancer patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of herbal products are safe when used as directed.
patients are not disclosing their use of herbal medicine to their physicians.

the evidence is insufficient for us to recommend the use of herbal products for any specific cancer-related purpose, and that patients should be counseled that the use of these products may be associated with significant risks.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of complementary/alternative products by cancer patients is common and that patients need to be educated about the potential risks associated with these products.
patients should be encouraged to talk to their health care providers about all the products and therapies they are using.
the use of complementary/alternative medicines is widespread and that oncologists should ask patients about their use of these medicines.
